config.title: cursor and pointer-events

intro.title: cursor and pointer-events
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple interactive webpage with buttons and links to learn how to control the mouse cursor and click behavior. You will use the CSS 'cursor' property to change the mouse pointer's appearance, such as turning it into a hand or a crosshair. You will also apply the 'pointer-events' property to enable or disable clicking on elements. By the end, you will understand how these properties enhance user experience and interactivity in web design.
intro.usecase: The cursor and pointer-events properties are essential for crafting intuitive and accessible interactive interfaces. In real-world applications, developers use these to provide visual feedback in dashboards—like changing the cursor to a 'grab' icon on draggable charts or to a 'not-allowed' symbol on disabled filter buttons. They also control clickability in complex UIs, such as making an overlay modal non-interactive with pointer-events: none while keeping its close button active. Mastering these CSS features ensures users can seamlessly navigate forms, menus, and panels with clear affordances, directly impacting usability and user experience.

objectives: Apply different cursor values to HTML elements to visually indicate interactive states
Configure pointer-events to control whether an element can be the target of mouse interactions
Construct interactive UI components by combining cursor and pointer-events properties
Manipulate element interactivity by toggling pointer-events between 'auto' and 'none' states
Implement custom cursor feedback for buttons, links, and form elements
Control layered element interactions by adjusting pointer-events on overlapping components
Update existing CSS rules to include cursor and pointer-events declarations

steps.title: Create a basic HTML structure for testing CSS cursor properties
steps.instruction: Create an HTML file with a <div> container that contains three child elements: a <button>, a <span>, and a <div> with nested text.
steps.hint: Start with a <div> as the main container. Inside it, add a <button> with text 'Click me', a <span> with text 'Hover over me', and another <div> with text 'Try to click me'.
steps.analogousExample:
/* Example HTML structure for testing */
Span element
Div element
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a basic HTML structure with three different elements to apply CSS cursor properties to in later steps.
successCriteria: The HTML contains a <div> container with exactly three child elements: a <button>, a <span>, and a <div> with text content.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the foundation for testing CSS cursor properties with multiple interactive elements.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have all three required elements: a button, a span, and a div with text inside the container.
steps.feedbackWrong: The HTML structure doesn't match the requirements. Please create a <div> container with a button, a span, and a div element inside.

steps.title: Add CSS file link and basic element styling
steps.instruction: Add a <link> element inside the <head> section of your HTML to connect a CSS file named 'styles.css', then add basic CSS rules to make the button, span, and div elements visible with distinct backgrounds.
steps.hint: Use <link rel='stylesheet' href='styles.css'> in the <head>. In the CSS file, target each element type and give them background colors like button { background-color: lightblue; }.
steps.expectedOutcome: The HTML file will link to a CSS file, and the CSS will apply basic styling to make the elements visible with background colors.
successCriteria: A <link> element with rel='stylesheet' and href='styles.css' is added to the <head>. CSS rules for button, span, and div with background-color properties are present.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully linked the CSS file and added basic styling to make the elements visible.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've made progress, but ensure you've added both the <link> in HTML and CSS rules for all three elements with background colors.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSS file isn't linked or styling is missing. Check that you added the <link> in <head> and CSS rules for button, span, and div.

steps.title: Apply the default cursor property to an element
steps.instruction: In your CSS file, add a rule that sets the cursor property to 'default' for the div element inside the body.
steps.hint: Use the CSS selector 'div' and the property 'cursor: default;' to apply the standard arrow cursor.
steps.expectedOutcome: The div element will have the standard arrow cursor when hovered.
successCriteria: The CSS contains a rule for 'div' with 'cursor: default;'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully applied the default cursor to the div element.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added 'cursor: default;' inside the div rule.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't seem right. Check that you've correctly written 'cursor: default;' for the div element.

steps.title: Use cursor: pointer; to indicate clickable elements
steps.instruction: In the CSS rule for the div, add the property cursor: pointer; to make it show a hand cursor when hovered.
steps.hint: Add cursor: pointer; inside the div's CSS rule. This will change the cursor to a hand icon when users hover over the element.
steps.expectedOutcome: The div element will display a hand cursor when hovered, indicating it's interactive.
successCriteria: The CSS rule for div includes cursor: pointer;
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added cursor: pointer; to make the div show a hand cursor on hover.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added cursor: pointer; inside the div's CSS rule.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSS rule for div doesn't include cursor: pointer;. Try adding it inside the div's rule.

steps.title: Experiment with different cursor values: text, move, and not-allowed
steps.instruction: Add a new CSS rule for a paragraph element and apply cursor: text; to it.
steps.hint: Create a new CSS selector for a paragraph element (p) and set its cursor property to 'text'.
steps.expectedOutcome: A paragraph element will show the text cursor when hovered over.
successCriteria: A CSS rule for a paragraph element is added with cursor: text;
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a text cursor to the paragraph element.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you've added a CSS rule for a paragraph element with cursor: text;
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSS rule for the paragraph element with cursor: text; is missing or incorrect.

steps.title: Create a disabled button element
steps.instruction: Add a CSS rule for a button element with a class of 'disabled-btn' that sets its background color to light gray (#ccc) and text color to dark gray (#666).
steps.hint: Use a class selector (.disabled-btn) and the properties background-color and color.
steps.expectedOutcome: A CSS rule for a disabled button element is created with appropriate styling.
successCriteria: The CSS contains a rule for .disabled-btn with background-color: #ccc; and color: #666;
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a disabled button style that will be used to demonstrate pointer-events.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added the button styling, but check that both background-color and color properties are correctly set.
steps.feedbackWrong: The disabled button styling is missing or incorrect. Make sure to use the class selector .disabled-btn with the specified colors.

steps.title: Apply pointer-events: none; to disable interactions
steps.instruction: Add a CSS rule for the disabled button element that sets pointer-events: none; to prevent mouse interactions.
steps.hint: Use the selector for your disabled button and add the pointer-events property with the value none.
steps.expectedOutcome: The disabled button will ignore all mouse events like clicks and hovers.
successCriteria: A CSS rule for the disabled button with pointer-events: none; is added.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully disabled pointer events on the button, preventing mouse interactions.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the correct selector and property value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSS rule for pointer-events: none; on the disabled button is missing or incorrect.

steps.title: Use pointer-events: auto; to restore default behavior
steps.instruction: Add a new CSS rule for the 'restore-btn' class that sets pointer-events to auto.
steps.hint: Use the property pointer-events: auto; to restore the default interactive behavior for an element.
steps.expectedOutcome: The restore button will regain its interactive capabilities, allowing clicks and hover effects.
successCriteria: A CSS rule for .restore-btn with pointer-events: auto; is added.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully used pointer-events: auto; to restore default interactive behavior.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added pointer-events: auto; to the .restore-btn rule.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSS rule for .restore-btn is missing or doesn't include pointer-events: auto;.

steps.title: Combine cursor and pointer-events on overlapping elements
steps.instruction: Add a new CSS rule for a .overlay element that sets cursor: not-allowed; and pointer-events: none;
steps.hint: Create a CSS class selector that targets .overlay and apply both properties inside the curly braces.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new CSS rule for .overlay will be created with both cursor and pointer-events properties applied together.
successCriteria: The .overlay selector exists and contains both cursor: not-allowed; and pointer-events: none; properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created an overlapping element style that combines cursor and pointer-events. This demonstrates how these properties work together to control both visual feedback and interaction behavior.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your .overlay rule includes both cursor: not-allowed; and pointer-events: none; properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSS rule for .overlay should include both cursor and pointer-events properties. Check that you've created a proper selector and included both properties with correct values.

steps.title: Create a custom cursor using URL
steps.instruction: Add a CSS rule for the .custom-cursor class that uses a custom cursor image with cursor: url('cursor.png'), auto;
steps.hint: The cursor property can accept a URL to an image file, followed by a fallback cursor keyword.
steps.expectedOutcome: The .custom-cursor class will be styled to use a custom cursor image with proper fallback.
successCriteria: The .custom-cursor rule includes cursor: url('cursor.png'), auto;
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a custom cursor rule. The cursor will display the specified image when hovering over elements with this class.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using the correct syntax: cursor: url('cursor.png'), auto;
steps.feedbackWrong: The custom cursor rule is missing or incorrect. Remember to use cursor: url('cursor.png'), auto; inside the .custom-cursor rule.

steps.title: Apply cursor: wait; for loading states
steps.instruction: Add a new CSS rule for a loading element that uses cursor: wait; to indicate processing.
steps.hint: Create a class selector like .loading and set its cursor property to wait.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new CSS rule with cursor: wait; is added to simulate a loading state.
successCriteria: The .loading selector exists and has cursor: wait; applied.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a loading cursor state. This visually indicates to users that the element is processing.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added the .loading rule, but make sure it includes cursor: wait; to show the loading indicator.
steps.feedbackWrong: The loading cursor rule isn't quite right. Create a .loading class with cursor: wait; to indicate processing.

steps.title: Review and test all cursor and pointer-events implementations
steps.instruction: Add a final comment summarizing the cursor and pointer-events properties you've implemented, then test them by hovering over the elements in your HTML.
steps.hint: Add a CSS comment at the end of your file that briefly describes the cursor and pointer-events properties you've used. Then open your HTML file in a browser to test the hover effects.
steps.analogousExample: /* Summary: cursor values control the mouse pointer appearance, pointer-events control interaction behavior */
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll see a summary comment in your CSS file and be able to test all cursor and pointer-events implementations by hovering over elements in your HTML.
successCriteria: A summary comment is added to the CSS file, and all cursor and pointer-events properties work correctly when hovering over elements in the browser.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! Your summary comment helps reinforce what you've learned about cursor and pointer-events properties. Testing them in the browser confirms they work as expected.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a comment, but make sure it summarizes the cursor and pointer-events properties. Also, test all elements by hovering over them in your HTML file.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try adding a CSS comment that summarizes the cursor and pointer-events properties you've implemented. Then open your HTML file in a browser to test the hover effects.
